title: How wine is made
lead: From vine to bottle: what shapes grapes in the vineyard, and the steps that turn them into white, red and rosé wine.

court.outcome: After studying this section, a student will understand the important factors that influence grape growing (viticulture) that impact the final flavor of the wine. After studying this section, a student will understand the definition of winemaking (vinification), the steps of making white, red, and rosé, and other important factors of consideration that influence the how and why wines taste the way they do.

intro.title: ONE GRAPE, THREE COLORS
intro.text: The big difference between white, rosé and red is how long the juice touches the skins. In most red grapes the color is in the skins, not the juice.

sections.name: The vine

lines.label: The plant
lines.text: Wine grapes grow on vines of the genus Vitis. Vitis vinifera is the species behind most quality wine, with about 10,000 varieties.

lines.label: The pest
lines.text: Phylloxera is a tiny vine louse. It wiped out many French vineyards in the mid-1800s. Vines are now grafted onto resistant American rootstock.

know: Vitis vinifera is native to the Mediterranean, Europe and Southwestern Asia.
Concord and Catawba are Vitis labrusca, not vinifera.
Phylloxera is fought with resistant American rootstock.
Varieties are chosen by wine law, climate, soil and marketability.
Regional wine laws often set which grapes are grown, and how.

sections.name: Climate, soil and terroir

lines.label: Climate
lines.text: Climate is the long-run weather of a place, not one year's weather. Most regions sit between 30 and 50 degrees latitude. Water, altitude and wind act as climate moderators.

lines.label: Soil
lines.text: Soil controls drainage, heat and nutrients. Growers match each grape to the soil that suits it. Terroir means every environmental effect on the vine.

know: Cool climates give tart fruit and more acidity; warm climates give riper fruit and less acidity.
Warmer grapes build more sugar, so the wine has more alcohol.
Macroclimate = region; mesoclimate = vineyard; microclimate = one vine.
Growing degree-days count days averaging above 50°F.
Climate moderators: altitude, diurnal shifts, sunshine hours, water, wind, rain shadow.

visuals.title: Soils the exam links to places

sections.name: The vineyard year

lines.label: The cycle
lines.text: The vine sleeps in winter, buds in spring, flowers, sets fruit and ripens. Veraison is when the berries change color. Harvest comes when the grapes are ripe. Each year’s crop, the vintage, differs with the weather.

lines.label: The work
lines.text: Growers prune in winter, manage leaves and water, and control yield. A green harvest drops unripe clusters so the rest ripen better.

know: Grapes do not keep ripening after they are picked.
Botrytis cinerea is a fungus that can be a good thing (noble rot).
Head training (gobelet/bush) and cordon training are the two main systems.
Yield is measured in tons per acre or hectoliters per hectare.
Brix measures sugar in the grapes.

sections.name: The winemaker’s choices

lines.label: Vinification
lines.text: Vinification is every decision made in the winery, from harvest to bottling. It starts with the winery’s goal, the style, the price point and local wine law.

lines.label: Vessels
lines.text: Wine ferments in wood, stainless steel or concrete. Size, shape, oxygen and temperature control all matter.

know: Vinification runs from harvest to bottling.
Must is unfermented grape juice.
Acidification adds acid to correct low acidity.
In Bordeaux and Burgundy, a wine can't be both chaptalized and acidified.
Whites usually ferment cooler than reds to keep delicate aromas.

visuals.title: Three ways to adjust the must

sections.name: Making white wine

lines.label: The steps
lines.text: Harvest, sort, crush and press. The juice ferments without the skins. Then the wine is fined or filtered and bottled.

lines.label: Keeping it fresh
lines.text: Whites are often picked cool and ferment cooler than reds to keep delicate aromas. Fermentation takes about two weeks.

know: White wine can be made from red grapes because the skins are left out.
Pressing comes before fermentation for whites.
Stopping fermentation early leaves residual sugar for an off-dry wine.
Fining agents such as egg white or bentonite clear out haze.

items.name: Harvest
items.text: Often picked in the cool of morning or night

items.name: Press
items.text: Juice goes straight off the skins

sections.name: Making red wine

lines.label: The steps
lines.text: Crush, then ferment the juice on its skins. Press, age, fine or filter, bottle, and sometimes age in bottle.

lines.label: Extraction
lines.text: Skins float to the top as a cap. Winemakers pump over or punch down to pull out color, flavor and tannin.

know: Red color comes from anthocyanin in black grape skins.
Pressing comes after fermentation for reds.
Pump-overs extract more; punch-downs are gentler.
Whole-cluster fermentation keeps stems and adds tannin (common with Pinot Noir).
Carbonic maceration ferments whole bunches under CO2 (think Beaujolais).

sections.name: Making rosé

lines.label: How
lines.text: Red grapes are crushed and left on their skins for a short time. The juice is then pressed off the skins and fermented.

lines.label: Color
lines.text: Contact time and pressing set the shade, from pale salmon to vivid pink.

know: Rosé color comes from brief contact with red grape skins.
The Court lists three methods: maceration time, blending and saignée.
Blending is often used for sparkling rosé.
The Court says saignée essentially doesn't exist anymore.

items.name: Saignée
items.text: 'Bleeding' juice off a red; rare today

sections.name: Oak, malolactic and lees

lines.label: Oak
lines.text: Oak adds vanilla, clove, smoke and coconut. It also lets in a little oxygen, which softens the wine. New barrels give more flavor than used ones.

lines.label: Malo and lees
lines.text: Malolactic fermentation turns sharp malic acid into soft lactic acid and can taste buttery. Lees are dead yeast; stirring them adds bready flavor and a creamy feel. As the dead yeast breaks down (autolysis), it adds richness and brioche aromas.

know: MLF is done by bacteria, not yeast, and lowers acidity.
Nearly all reds and some whites (Chardonnay, Viognier) go through MLF.
Bigger barrels give less oak flavor and oxygen.
American oak is Quercus alba; European oak is Quercus petraea.
Chaptalization is adding sugar to must to raise alcohol.

sections.name: Bottling and packaging

lines.label: Clearing the wine
lines.text: Before bottling, wine is clarified. Fining adds an agent that pulls particles down; filtering pushes wine through a screen or pad.

lines.label: The package
lines.text: Wine goes into bottles, kegs or boxes. It is sealed with cork, a composite, a screw cap (Stelvin) or a glass top (Vinolok).

know: Fining agents like bentonite, egg whites or gelatin settle out particles.
Filtering pushes wine through a screen or pad.
Stelvin is a screw cap; Vinolok is a glass top.
Containers include bottles, kegs and boxed wine.
Labels must follow government label laws.

Must is unfermented grape juice; lees are dead yeast left after fermentation.

facts.fact: Viticulture is the factors of production that influence grape growing: factors from nature plus man-made decisions in the vineyard that affect wine quality.
Common types of viticulture listed by the Court: organic, biodynamic, sustainable, dry farming.
Climate is the weather of an area in general or over a long period (temperature, humidity, rainfall, sunshine, wind and more). The Court stresses that climate and weather are different.
Climate types: continental, maritime, Mediterranean, desert/arid. Climate descriptors: cool, moderate, warm, hot.
Macroclimate is the climate of an area such as a wine region; mesoclimate is the climate of a vineyard; microclimate is the climate around a single vine.
Growing degree-days are counted for days in the growing season when the average temperature is over 50°F.
Most wine-growing regions lie between 30 and 50 degrees latitude; regions outside this band exist mainly because of climate moderators.
Climate moderators: altitude, diurnal shifts, sunshine hours, bodies of water, wind, rain shadow effect. Examples named include San Pablo Bay, the Benguela Current and the Humboldt Current.
Topography is the surface features of the land: elevation, mountains, hills, valleys and bodies of water.

Soil properties that matter to the vine: drainage or water retention, sun reflection, nutrient content, temperature regulation, pest resistance. Soil examples: clay, slate, limestone, granite, chalk, sand, schist.
Soils are matched to grape varieties based on climate and the needs of the variety.
Bordeaux soils: gravel, clay, limestone, sand. Varieties are matched to soil, for example Cabernet Sauvignon in gravel and Merlot in clay.
Chablis and Côte d'Or soils: limestone, clay. Beaujolais: granite.
Champagne soils: limestone, chalk. Grapes are picked earlier to preserve natural acidity.
Mosel soil: slate. Steep, south-facing hillsides maximize sun exposure and warmth.
Coonawarra soil: terra rossa.

Grapes are the fruit of a vining plant of the genus Vitis. Vitis vinifera is native to the Mediterranean, Europe and Southwestern Asia, is the most common for quality grape production, and has about 10,000 varieties (e.g. Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay, Riesling, Syrah).
Vitis labrusca examples: Catawba, Concord.
Parts of the grape vine: rootstock, trunk, cordons, shoots/canes, grape clusters/bunches, canopy.
Grape varieties are chosen by regional wine law, climate compatibility, soil compatibility and marketability.
Every year produces a different crop called the vintage; each vintage can indicate style, quality and price potential. Introductory students do not need to memorize vintage differences.
Vineyard management covers canopy management (managing leaf growth), irrigation, pests and disease, and managing yield.
Botrytis cinerea is a fungus/mold that 'can be a good thing!'. Phylloxera is a pest.
Green harvest: a quality measure of removing or dropping unripe grapes or clusters.
Vine cycle: dormancy, bud break, flowering, fruit set, ripening (veraison, hang time), maturity, harvest, pruning.
Two main vine training systems: head training (e.g. gobelet/bush) and cordon training (using support for growth).

Phylloxera is a microscopic vine louse that destroyed many of France's vineyards in the mid-19th century. Resistant American vine rootstock is used to stop the spread; most wine regions of the world are affected.
Yield is how much fruit a vine produces, measured in tons per acre or hectoliters per hectare.
Harvest timing depends on weather, wine style, producer goals, regional wine law and number of picking passes. Grapes are picked by hand or by machine. Sugar is measured with scales such as Brix.
Terroir ('goût de terroir', taste of earth) covers all of the environmental impacts on a grapevine.
Bud break happens in April/May (Sept/Oct in the Southern Hemisphere); hail can destroy the delicate buds.
Young clusters appear in June and July (Nov/Dec in the Southern Hemisphere). In mid to late summer the berries change color and ripen: veraison.
Harvest usually falls between September and November, or February to May in the Southern Hemisphere. Grapes do not continue to ripen once picked.
Winter pruning, when the pruner cuts back the prior year's canes, is one of the most expensive and important vineyard jobs.
Most of the world's quality wine comes from Vitis vinifera; by about the third year a vine can produce fruit of proper quality for winemaking. 'Old vines' has no official definition.
Warm climates generally give riper fruit flavors and less acidity; cool climates give tart fruit flavors and more acidity.
White wine grapes are picked earlier in the season than red wine grapes.
Warmer-climate grapes build higher sugar levels, which make higher-alcohol wines; cooler-climate grapes have lower sugar and keep more acidity.
Vinification: decisions and practices made in the winery from harvest to bottling.

Winemaking starts with harvest, sort, destem. White: crush, press, fermentation, fining/filtering, bottling. Red: crush, maceration, fermentation with skin contact, pressing, aging, fining/filtration, bottling, bottle aging. Rosé: crush red grapes, short skin contact, pressing, fermentation, fining/filtration, bottling.

Three types of rosé production: maceration time, blending (often used for sparkling wine), and saignée. The Court says saignée ('bleeding') essentially doesn't exist anymore; it was a red-wine concentration technique with rosé as the byproduct.
Alcoholic fermentation: sugar + yeast gives alcohol, CO2, heat, aromas and flavors. Saccharomyces cerevisiae is the yeast species for wine fermentation.
Aging can be on the lees or without, in concrete, stainless steel or oak. Fermentation vessels: wood, stainless steel, concrete.
Barrel sizes: barrique 225 liters, puncheon 300 liters, demi-muid 600 liters, foudre/botti 1,000+ liters. Other woods used for barrels include acacia, cherry and chestnut.
Winemaking terms listed: grape must, chaptalization, acidification, water addition, lees, autolysis, malolactic fermentation, carbonic maceration.
Chaptalization: adding sugar to unfermented grape must to increase alcohol after fermentation; used when grapes do not reach enough sugar ripeness.
Closures listed: cork, composites, screw cap (Stelvin), glass top (Vinolok).
White wine can be made from red or white grapes because the skins are not used in fermentation; most white wines use green and yellow grapes.
Picking in the morning or at night gives fresher-tasting white wines. Grapes go straight to the press, and the juice settles before fermentation.
A white wine takes about 14 days to ferment; whites ferment cooler than reds to keep delicate floral aromas.
Stopping the yeast before all the sugar is eaten (usually by chilling) leaves 'residual sugar' for an off-dry wine.
Fining agents (casein, egg whites, bentonite clay) remove proteins that make wine cloudy; filtering follows.
Red winemaking differs in one important way: the juice ferments with the grape skins. All red color comes from anthocyanin in black grape skins.
Whole-cluster fermentation keeps the stems, which adds tannin. Pinot Noir often ferments with whole clusters, Cabernet Sauvignon does not.
Floating skins (the 'cap') are kept in contact by pumping over (stronger extraction, rich reds) or punching down (gentler, more subtle reds).
Most wines take 5 to 21 days to ferment. After fermentation the skins are pressed, giving about 15% more wine.
Red wines age in barrels, concrete, glass, clay or steel; wooden barrels affect wine most noticeably.
In most red grape varieties, the pigments that give red wine its color come from the skins, not the juice.
Rosé gets its color from brief contact with red grape skins; contact time and pressing set the shade from pale salmon to vivid pink.
Malolactic fermentation (MLF) converts tart malic acid into softer lactic acid. It is done by bacteria (Oenococcus oeni), not yeast, and lowers acidity.
The bacteria release diacetyl, which gives buttery or creamy aromas.
Nearly all red wines and some white wines (such as Chardonnay and Viognier) go through MLF.
Lees are dead yeast particles. Stirring them adds bread- or beer-like flavor and a creamier texture.
Oak adds flavors such as vanilla, clove, smoke and coconut; lets in oxygen slowly, making wine smoother and less astringent; and gives a home for MLF.
Oak flavor extraction drops each time a barrel is reused. Larger barrels give less oak lactone and oxygen; barriques are 225 liters, botti and foudres about 1,000 to 20,000 liters.
The two main oak species are Quercus alba (American white oak) and Quercus petraea (European white oak). American oak suits bolder wines; European oak suits lighter wines.
Location and geography considerations for a vineyard (Introductory): site location of the vineyard, goals of the wine producer, regional wine laws, financial considerations.
Regional wine laws dictate which grape varieties can be grown, and how they are grown, in many wine regions of the world.

Vineyards are managed to stay viable and healthy; vines are trained to a size and shape that ripens grapes best, and many training systems exist. Irrigation makes sure the vine has enough water in the growing season.
Harvest (Introductory): grapes are collected in large or small bins; ripeness is a range, and one vineyard manager's definition of ripeness may differ from another's; structure and flavor ripeness.

Rhône soils (Introductory column): Northern Rhône decomposed granite and schist; Southern Rhône galets, alluvial, limestone. The Introductory outcome asks students to know the famous soil type of the Southern Rhône.
Viticulture soil row (Introductory): be able to match soils to Champagne, Chablis, Côte d'Or, Haut-Médoc, Pomerol, St.-Émilion, Châteauneuf-du-Pape and Mosel.
Factors in winemaking decisions: the goal of the winery, the style of wine, the price point, regional wine laws the winery must follow, and sustainability.
Fermentation vessel considerations (Introductory): size (large or small), shape (oval, round, egg), oxygen permeability, temperature control.

Winemaking decisions (Introductory): temperature control and why it matters for different colors and styles; oxygen management and its impact on the final style; extraction through punch downs, pump overs, maceration times and fermentation temperature.
Aging and maturation considerations (Introductory): costs, age of barrels, length of time of aging.
Preparation for bottling (Introductory): clarification and the difference between fining and filtration. Cold stabilization, fining agent examples and sulfur additions are Certified-column.

Packaging (Introductory): containers are bottles, kegs and boxed wine; closures are cork, composites, screw cap (Stelvin) and glass top (Vinolok); packaging covers labels and label design, capsule colors and design, and adhering to governmental label laws.
Must: the unfermented juice of grapes extracted by crushing or pressing; grape juice in the cask or vat before it is converted into wine.

Acidification: the addition of acid to wine by a winemaker to balance the soft components (sugar, alcohol, fruit). It is legal in some areas to correct deficient acidity. It is illegal in Bordeaux and Burgundy to both chaptalize and acidify a wine.
Fining: clarifying wine with agents such as bentonite (powdered clay), isinglass, casein, gelatin or egg whites, which combine with sediment particles so they settle to the bottom and can be removed.

Filtering: pumping wine through a screen or pad to remove leftover grape and fermentation particles. Most wines are filtered for clarity and stability, though some winemakers believe flavor and complexity may be stripped.

Autolysis: enzymes break down dead yeast cells in the lees, releasing amino acids, proteins and carbohydrates. It gives richness, creaminess and aromas of bread dough, toast or brioche, and is a key element of traditional-method sparkling wine such as Champagne.

Carbonic maceration: most associated with Beaujolais; makes light-bodied, fresh, fruity reds. Whole bunches go into a tank where oxygen is displaced by carbon dioxide, and fermentation starts inside the berry. In practice the bottom grapes are crushed and ferment with yeast, so the wine is partly carbonic and partly traditional fermentation.
Australia's Food Standards Code: water may be added only to dilute high-sugar grape must before fermentation, to help fermentation, and not below 13.5 degrees Baumé.

unverified: Resolved Nov 2, 2026: 'grape must' is now defined from the Wine Spectator glossary (unfermented juice before it becomes wine).
Definitions of hybrid, crossing, clone and mutation: listed as terms in the Court's curriculum guide, but no definitions were found in the sources fetched, so they are left out.
Puncheon and demi-muid sizes come only from the Court's guide; no second source was checked.

Resolved Nov 2, 2026 by reading the PDF pages: macro/meso/microclimate, growing degree-days, parts of the vine, the vine cycle, training systems, Vitis labrusca, the three rosé methods, barrel sizes, other barrel woods and whole-cluster are Certified-column detail. They stay as extra context but are beyond Level 1.
Wine Folly timings (14 days for whites, 5–21 days for reds, 15% more wine from pressing, harvest months) are secondary-source generalizations, not Court figures.
Water addition: only Australia's rule (Wine Australia) was checked; US and EU rules were not.
The Court lists 'diurnal shifts' and 'rain shadow effect' as moderators without defining them; this chapter names them but does not define them.

read.where: Wine grapes grow on vines of the genus **Vitis**. The species behind most quality wine is **Vitis vinifera**, native to the Mediterranean, Europe and Southwestern Asia. It has about **10,000 varieties**. **Viticulture** is grape growing: what nature gives plus the grower’s decisions, which together shape the wine’s quality.

Climates are also described as **cool**, **moderate**, **warm** or **hot**.

stops.name: Cool vs. warm
stops.text: Cool climates give **tart fruit** and **more acidity**. Warm climates give riper fruit and less acidity. Warmer grapes build more sugar, so the wine has **more alcohol**.

stops.name: Moderators and topography
stops.text: **Climate moderators** change a place’s climate: **altitude**, **diurnal shifts**, **sunshine hours**, **bodies of water**, **wind** and the **rain shadow** effect. **Topography** is the shape of the land: elevation, mountains, hills, valleys and water.

stops.name: Big to small
stops.text: **Macroclimate** is a whole wine region. **Mesoclimate** is one vineyard. **Microclimate** is the space around a single vine.

stops.name: Soil
stops.text: Soil affects drainage, temperature and nutrients, so growers match each grape to a soil. In Bordeaux, **Cabernet Sauvignon** goes in **gravel** and **Merlot** in **clay**. Soil can drain or hold water, reflect sun, feed the vine, hold heat and resist pests. The Southern Rhône’s famous soil is **galets**.

stops.name: Terroir
stops.text: **Terroir** covers every environmental effect on the vine. The French phrase is **goût de terroir**, the taste of earth.

read.visualIntro: Soils the exam ties to famous places:
read.mixup: **Mesoclimate** is one vineyard. **Microclimate** is the space around a single vine.

read.bigIdea: Every year, the vine runs through the same cycle.
read.where: The vine rests through winter, then buds in spring. It flowers, sets fruit, ripens and is picked. Each year’s crop is called the **vintage**. Each vintage can differ in style, quality and price because of the weather. You don’t need to memorize vintages at Level 1.
read.stopsTitle: The year, in the Northern Hemisphere

stops.name: Bud break
stops.text: The buds open. **Hail** can destroy these delicate buds.

stops.name: Veraison
stops.text: Young clusters form in June and July. Then the berries **change color** and ripen: that’s **veraison**.

stops.name: The grower’s work
stops.text: Growers manage the **canopy** (the leaves), water, pests and **yield**. A **green harvest** drops unripe clusters for quality. Vines are **trained** to a size and shape that ripens grapes best, and **irrigation** makes sure they get enough water.

stops.name: Harvest
stops.text: Timing depends on weather, wine style and local wine law. Sugar is measured with scales like **Brix**. Grapes don’t keep ripening once they’re picked. Grapes are picked **by hand** or **by machine** and collected in large or small bins. Ripeness is a range: two growers may call different grapes ripe.

stops.name: Pruning
stops.text: The pruner cuts back last year’s canes. It’s one of the most expensive and important jobs in the vineyard.

read.bigIdea: Every wine starts with the winery’s plan.
read.where: **Vinification** is every decision made in the winery, from **harvest** to **bottling**. The Court lists the questions that come first: the winery’s **goal**, the **style** of wine, its **price point**, any **regional wine laws**, and **sustainability**.

stops.name: The vessel
stops.text: Wine ferments in **wood**, **stainless steel** or **concrete**. Vessels can be large or small, and oval, round or **egg**-shaped. The Court asks you to weigh how much **oxygen** each lets in and how well it controls **temperature**.

stops.name: Temperature
stops.text: The Court wants you to know why **temperature control** matters for each color and style. Whites usually ferment **cooler** than reds to keep delicate floral aromas.

stops.name: Oxygen
stops.text: How much **oxygen** the wine meets changes its final style. Oak barrels, for example, let oxygen in slowly, which makes the wine smoother.

stops.name: Fixing the must
stops.text: **Must** is the unfermented juice. **Chaptalization** adds sugar for more alcohol. **Acidification** adds acid for balance. **Water addition** dilutes very sweet must: Australia allows it before fermentation, down to 13.5° Baumé.

read.visualIntro: Three ways to adjust the must:
read.mixup: **Chaptalization** adds sugar to the must. **Acidification** adds acid.

read.bigIdea: White wine is juice fermented without the skins.
read.where: Every wine starts with **harvest**, **sort** and **destem**. For whites, the grapes are crushed and **pressed**, and the juice ferments without the skins. That’s why white wine can be made from red or white grapes.

stops.name: Harvest
stops.text: Picking in the morning or at night gives fresher-tasting whites.

stops.name: Press
stops.text: The grapes go straight to the press. The juice settles before it ferments.

stops.name: Ferment
stops.text: Yeast (**Saccharomyces cerevisiae**) turns sugar into alcohol, CO2 and heat: **alcoholic fermentation**. Whites ferment cooler than reds to keep delicate floral aromas. Stop the yeast early, usually by chilling, and some **residual sugar** stays for an off-dry wine.

stops.name: Fine and filter
stops.text: **Fining** agents like egg whites or bentonite clay remove the proteins that make wine cloudy. Then the wine is filtered and bottled.

keyPoints.line: give red wine its color, from a pigment called anthocyanin.
comes after fermentation for red wine.

read.bigIdea: Red wine ferments with its skins.
read.where: In most red grapes the color is in the skins, not the juice. So the juice ferments on its skins, which give color from a pigment called **anthocyanin**. **Pressing comes after fermentation**, the reverse of white wine.

stops.name: Crush and macerate
stops.text: The grapes are crushed and soak with their skins (**maceration**), then ferment together. Keeping the stems in (**whole-cluster**) adds tannin. Pinot Noir often ferments this way; Cabernet Sauvignon does not.

stops.name: Work the cap
stops.text: The skins float up and form a **cap**. **Pumping over** gives stronger extraction for rich reds. **Punching down** is gentler, for more subtle reds. The Court lists four levers for **extraction**: punch downs, pump overs, maceration time and fermentation temperature.

stops.name: Press
stops.text: Most wines take 5 to 21 days to ferment. Then the skins are pressed, which gives about 15% more wine.

stops.name: Age and bottle
stops.text: Reds age in barrels, concrete, glass, clay or steel. Wooden barrels change the wine the most. Then the wine is fined or filtered and bottled.

stops.name: Carbonic maceration
stops.text: Whole bunches go into a tank filled with **carbon dioxide**, and fermentation starts **inside each berry**. It makes light, fresh, fruity reds and is most linked to **Beaujolais**.

read.bigIdea: Rosé is red grapes with a short time on the skins.
read.where: Red grapes are crushed and left on their skins for a short time. Then the juice is pressed off the skins and fermented. Contact time and pressing set the color, from **pale salmon** to **vivid pink**.

stops.name: Maceration
stops.text: The juice sits on red skins for a short time, then it’s pressed and fermented.

stops.name: Blending
stops.text: The Court says **blending** is often used for **sparkling wine**.

stops.name: Saignée
stops.text: **Saignée** was a way to concentrate a red wine, with rosé as the byproduct. The Court says it essentially doesn’t exist anymore.

read.sayIt: It’s made from red grapes, with just a little time on the skins.

read.bigIdea: Oak, malo and lees add flavor and texture.
read.where: Wine can age **on its lees** or without them, in **oak**, **stainless steel** or **concrete**. Oak, malolactic fermentation and lees each leave their own mark on the wine.

stops.name: Oak
stops.text: New oak adds **vanilla**, **clove**, **smoke** and **coconut**. It lets in oxygen slowly, so the wine gets smoother. Oak flavor drops each time a barrel is reused, and **bigger barrels** give less.

stops.name: Two oaks
stops.text: **American oak** (Quercus alba) suits bolder wines. **European oak** (Quercus petraea) suits lighter wines.

stops.name: Malolactic
stops.text: **Bacteria**, not yeast, turn tart **malic acid** into softer **lactic acid**. It lowers acidity and can smell **buttery** or creamy. Nearly all reds and some whites, like **Chardonnay** and Viognier, go through it.

stops.name: Lees
stops.text: **Lees** are dead yeast particles. Stirring them adds bread- or beer-like flavor and a **creamier** texture. As the dead yeast breaks down (**autolysis**), it adds richness, creaminess and bread-dough or brioche aromas. It’s key to traditional-method sparkling wine like Champagne.

stops.name: How long, and in what
stops.text: Aging choices weigh **cost**, the **age of the barrels** and **how long** the wine ages. Oak flavor drops each time a barrel is reused.

read.mixup: **Alcoholic fermentation** uses yeast to turn sugar into alcohol. **Malolactic** uses bacteria to turn malic acid into lactic acid.
read.sayIt: It sees some oak, so expect a little vanilla and spice.

read.bigIdea: Before it’s sold, wine is cleared, sealed and labeled.
read.where: Before bottling, most wine is **clarified**. The Court wants you to know the difference between **fining** and **filtration**. Then the winery picks a container, a closure and a label.

stops.name: Fining
stops.text: **Fining** adds an agent such as **bentonite** clay, **egg whites**, gelatin, casein or isinglass. It binds to the haze and sinks, so it can be removed.

stops.name: Filtering
stops.text: **Filtering** pumps wine through a screen or pad to remove leftover grape and yeast bits. Most wines are filtered for clarity and stability, though some winemakers think it strips flavor.

stops.name: Containers
stops.text: Wine is sold in **bottles**, **kegs** and **boxed wine**.

stops.name: Closures
stops.text: **Cork**, **composites**, **screw cap** (**Stelvin**) and **glass top** (**Vinolok**).

stops.name: Labels
stops.text: Label design and **capsule** color are the winery’s choice, but every label must follow **government label laws**.
